We were alone there, he and I, Inhabiting the empty street. Under a sign for Natural Bloom Cigars, While lights clicked softly in the dusk from red to green, He stopped and gazed into a window Where a plaster Venus, modeling a truss, Looked out at Eastbound traffic. Somewhere in Chelsea, in early summer, walking through the twilight toward the docks, I thought I made out Robinson ahead of me. From an uncurtained second-story room, a radio was playing “There’s a Small Hotel”; a kite twisted above dark rooftops and slow-drifting birds.

We were alone there, he and I, inhabiting the empty street. Beneath a sign for Natural Bloom Cigars, while the lights clicked softly in the dusk from red to green, he stopped and gazed into a window, where a plaster Venus, modeling a truss, looked out at eastbound traffic.

(But Robinson, I knew, was out of town: he summers at a place in Maine—sometimes on Fire Island, sometimes the Cape—leaves town in June, and returns after Labor Day.)

And yet, I almost called out, “Robinson!”

There was no chance. Just as I passed, turning my head to search his face, his head turned with mine and fixed me with dilated, terrifying eyes that stopped my blood. His voice came at me like an echo in the dark:

“I thought I saw the whirlpool opening. Kicked all night at a bolted door. You must have followed me from Astor Place. An empty paper floats down at the last. And then a day as huge as yesterday in pairs unrolled its horror on my face until it blocked—”
outputs.L2:
In Chelsea at the start of summer, I was heading toward the waterfront at dusk when I believed I spotted Robinson walking in front of me. Music from *There’s a Small Hotel* drifted out of an upstairs room whose windows had no curtains. Over the shadowed roofs and gently gliding birds, a kite spun in the air.

The deserted street seemed to belong only to the two of us. Beneath an advertisement for Natural Bloom Cigars, with the traffic signals quietly changing from red to green in the fading light, he paused before a shopwindow. Inside stood a plaster figure of Venus wearing a medical truss and facing the cars traveling east.

I knew, however, that Robinson had left the city. Every June he goes away for the summer—to Maine, Fire Island, or Cape Cod—and does not return until after Labor Day. Even so, I nearly shouted his name, though there was no possibility that the man could truly be him.

As I drew level and turned to examine his face, he moved his head at exactly the same moment. His enlarged, dreadful eyes locked onto mine and made my blood run cold. Then his words reached me as though reverberating through darkness: he said he had imagined a whirlpool beginning to open; that he had spent the entire night kicking against a locked door; that I must have trailed him from Astor Place; that, at the very end, a blank sheet of paper drifted downward. After that, a day as immense as the one before it, doubled into pairs, spread its terror across his face until it shut out—
